title: Enhancing mechanical properties and wear resistance of dual phase steel through surface mechanical attrition treatment
abstract: The study investigates the mechanical properties of dual-phase (DP) steel undergoing surface martensite transformation through Surface Mechanical Attrition Treatment, revealing phase transformation and grain refinement, increasing exponentially with treatment duration. After 40 min of SMAT, X-ray Diffraction (XRD) and Scanning Electron Microscopy (SEM) analyses revealed approximately 37% martensite and 63% ferrite phases, in contrast to 5% martensite and 95% ferrite phases in the as-received state. The surface hardness of the steel increased to 270 VH0.05 (up from 145 VH0.05), while the yield strength rose to 405 MPa (up from 258 MPa). Furthermore, a 60% reduction in the specific wear rate of the steel was achieved. This study highlights SMAT as an innovative method for tailoring the microstructure of steel and enhancing its mechanical properties through stress-induced phase transformation.

sections.heading: Introduction
paragraphs: Dual-phase (DP) steel, a strong and ductile material, is commonly used in automotive and structural applications. However, it faces challenges in industrial settings, such as limited wear resistance, fatigue strength, and limited corrosion resistance. The softer ferrite phase in DP steel may be more prone to wear, while the harder martensite phase provides strength. The material's cyclic loading can lead to fatigue failure, and its formability can be limited during complex manufacturing processes. These issues may limit the performance and lifespan of DP steels in certain industrial applications. Surface Mechanical Attrition Treatment (SMAT) is a surface treatment process that enhances the properties of materials like DP steel through mechanical impacts. SMAT involves surface hardening, which increases dislocation density and strengthens the material's surface layer through strain hardening. This process also introduces residual compressive stresses, which counteract tensile stresses that lead to crack initiation and propagation, enhancing the fatigue life of the material. For enhancing the qualities of material surfaces, SMAT is continuously gaining popularity in this field. ( Lu and Lu, 1999 ;  Wang et al., 2006 ;  Tao et al., 2002 ). Studies have shown that this technology can be used to produce surface nano-crystallization ( Zhang et al., 2003 ;  Chen et al., 2005 ), functionally gradient microstructures ( Sun et al., 2017 ;  Guo et al., 2017 ), coating ( Revesz and Takacs, 2007 ;  Eidivandi et al., 2020 ), boronizing ( Balusamy et al., 2012 ), carburization ( Sahu and Sasikumar, 2017 ,  2019 ), and nano-composites ( Samavatian et al., 2020 ). This technology continuously injects steel or ceramic balls at a very high speed using high-pressure air or water jets, revolving impellors, and vibration. The impact of steel balls on surfaces causes the necessary plastic deformation of the materials. They have been applied extensively to strengthen metal surfaces. Because of the residual compressive stresses that the material retains, the layer becomes work-hardened, resulting in surfaces with a higher level of fatigue or wear resistance ( Tadge and Sasikumar, 2018 ). Grain sizes that range from nanometers at the surface to micrometers at the core can be used to generate gradient microstructures. Consequently, various mechanical properties are formed, such as a hard metal surface and tough core. Surfaces in SMAT processes undergo significant plastic deformation because of the continuous collision of high-energy balls. The surface layers deform plastically under large stresses (>0.6) and high strain rates (>10 −2  per second) ( Chan et al., 2010 ). This increased strain caused by SMAT in some metals and alloys leads to grain refinement and martensite transformation, which provide a nano-crystalline surface ( Kalhor et al., 2020 ;  Tao et al., 2009 ;  Challa et al., 2014 ).

Researchers developed mathematical models to find out strain induced martensitic (α′) transformation using the effects of applied stress and stacking fault energy (SFE) on the formation of shear bands ( Byun, 2003 ;  Cherkaoui et al., 1998 ). The models predict strain induced martensite transformation for increased applied stress/strain, strain rate and low temperature. Further, the SFE strongly influences the phase transformation. Low stacking fault energy materials such as stainless steel is prone to undergo strain induced martensitic transformation, while mechanical twinning is favored in metals with high SFE ( Cherkaoui et al., 1998 ). The strain induced martensitic (α’) are reported to have BCC or BCT structure Pun et al., 2022 . The transformation sequence is reported as

During SMAT, materials with high SFE accumulate strain and form dislocation cells and walls, thereby dividing coarse grains into smaller parts. The deformation mechanism may shift from slip to mechanical twinning in low SFE materials, especially at low temperatures and strain rates ( Wan et al., 2001 ;  Zhang et al., 2011 ). In a study on austenitic stainless 316 L,  Wan et al. (2001)  observed mechanical twinning and martensite phase formation. The authors have shown that the phase transformation is possible in materials with low SFE. It is showed that by modifying the microstructure the yield strength could be doubled in a stainless steel. The SMAT-treated steel exhibits a significantly higher hardness at the surface, approximately 2–3 times greater than that of the as-annealed steel. Cross-sectional microstructural studies depicted a gradient microstructure in grain size in the SMAT-treated steel, ranging from ∼50 nm at the surface to ∼20 μm at the core. Researchers identified alternating layers of nano-band austenite and nano-lamellar martensite in a stainless steel.

Dual-phase steels, Complex phase (CP) steels, transformation induced plasticity (TRIP) steels, twinning induced plasticity (TWIP) steels are designed in such way that they undergo strain induced transformation when exposed to stress ( Bhadeshia, 2017 ). In the present study we investigate the martensitic phase transformation induced in a DP steels through surface mechanical attrition treatment. In addition to being highly strong, hard and wear resistant, it has attracted a great deal of attention due to its ability to sustain extremely abrasive environments, such as mining drills, slurry pumps, ball bearings, die-casting and milling cutters, and for a wide range of manufacturing applications ( Cherkaoui et al., 2000 ;  Srivastava et al., 2020 ;  Nouroozi et al., 2018 ;  Mazaheri et al., 2014 ;  Zhang et al., 2015 ;  Tasan et al., 2015 ;  Koh-ichi et al., 1997 ). We are studying the effect of strain-induced phase transformation on dual-phase steel with SMAT. Furthermore, this study has attempted to modify the mechanical and tribological properties of DP steel through the use of SMAT to modify the surface microstructure.

sections.heading: Material
paragraphs:
Table 1 
                          describes the chemical composition of the steel that was employed in the current study.

The steel used in this study is a dual-phase steel with ultra-low carbon content, there are no carbon atoms in the interstitial sites. Mn addition strengthens these steels' tendencies for strain hardening. These steels have low yield strength, high plastic strain ratio, high strain rate sensitivity, and superior formability due to their low carbon content. The heat treatment causes martensite to develop, which gives the steel a high yield strength and improved strain hardening tendency ( Nouroozi et al., 2018 ). As received, the dual-phase steel contained both martensite and ferrite. The steel sheets were delivered with a controlled annealing heat treatment and had a thickness of 2 mm. These sheets were sliced into 150 (L) × 30 (W) × 2 (T) mm samples, and the surfaces were cleaned to remove any oxides, dirt, and oil or grease.

sections.heading: Surface Mechanical Attrition Treatment (SMAT)
paragraphs: Industrial shot peening equipment was used to apply SMAT to the steel samples. For this application, chrome alloy steel shots no. (S390) having hardness (52 HRC) was used. Using compressed air technology, the shot-peening equipment continuously strikes steel balls onto the samples. It comprises a dust collection chamber, a suction and recirculation unit to gather and re-inject the steel shots, and a sample attachment stage. The throwing velocity is around 60 m/s, and the operating distance between the sample and the nozzle is approximately 300 mm. The steel samples were subjected to continuous bombardment of shots for different durations 10, 20, 30, and 40 min, respectively. These fixed parameters were determined by our previous published article [ Katiyar and Sasikumar, 2024 ].

sections.heading: Characterization techniques
paragraphs: An optical emission spectrometer (OES) LECO GDS 500 A was used to analyze the chemical composition of steel. A JEOL JSM 6390 A scanning electron microscope (SEM) was used to examine the microstructures of steel before and after SMAT. With a Microvickers hardness tester (Omni Tech, India), the altered surface and cross-sectional hardness caused by the process are examined. To confirm the hardness of the treated layer, the tests were run at a 50 g weight. A BRUKER D2 PHASER x-ray diffractometer (operated with Cu-Kα radiation at 30 KV and 20 mA) was used to examine the dislocation densities, lattice structure, and phase component changes. Using a UTM (MECHATRONIC CONTROL SYSTEM) machine, the impacts of SMAT on the mechanical properties were investigated. An experiment was performed to determine the change in Young's modulus of steel during bending. The PIN ON DISC dry wear testing machine assessed the wear behavior of steel.

sections.heading: XRD analysis
paragraphs:
Fig. 1 
                          shows the typical x-ray diffraction pattern of the steel samples before and after 10, 20, 30 and 40 min of surface mechanical attrition treatment respectively. The x-axis is break and magnified to show the phase transformation due to SMAT. As depicted in  Fig. 1  the XRD analysis evidently showed ferrite and martensite phases in untreated condition and the transformation into martensite phases after SMAT. A Rietveld analysis of the x-ray patterns was carried out using XPERT HIGH SCORE PLUS software to quantify the phases. The x-ray spectrum of the untreated steel reveals characteristic peaks at 44.7 o corresponding to the reflections of (110) plane of ferrite phase (ICDD 00-006-0696) and at 45.4° corresponding to (101) plane of martensite phase (ICDD 00-044-1292). The phase quantification using Rietveld analysis showed about 5% martensite and 95% ferrite in untreated condition. The percent transformation after 40 min of SMAT is determined as 37% martensite and 63% ferrite. It is reported that the materials with high SFE undergo grain refinement while the one with low SFE undergo phase transformation ( Wan et al., 2001 ;  Zhang et al., 2011 ). The SFE of low carbon, high Mn steel are reported as 8–13.5 mJ/m 2  ( Gubicza, 2017 ). Thus, the martensite transformation of DP steels could be attributed to low due to low stacking energy, larger applied stress and high strain rate.

sections.heading: Microstructure100
paragraphs:
Fig. 2 (a) 
                          shows the typical cross sectional microstructures at different magnifications and  Fig. 2 (b–e) shows the typical surface microstructures of the steel subjected to 0, 10, 30 and 40 min of SMAT respectively.  Fig. 2 a illustrates the regions that were severely plastically deformed and unaffected by SMAT after 40 min. The slip bands are visible in the deformed region and the depth of these regions found varying. The cross sectional microstructure magnified image ( Fig. 2 a) shows carbide precipitates between lath type martensite. The surface microstructure of the steel prior to SMAT shows equiaxed grains of polygonal ferrite and minor amount (5%) of martensite. The initial grain size is about 45 μm and the ferrite grain size is refined significantly by SMAT. The microstructure of steel subjected to SMAT evidently shows stress induced phase transformation i.e. transformation to martensite. The percent transformation into martensite is found to be about 37% after 40 min of SMAT as confirmed by XRD.

sections.heading: Hardness profile
paragraphs:
The hardness variations across the cross section is also obtained and delineated in  Fig. 3 
                         . The SEM cross sectional images is also given as inset. The surface hardness of the steel is increased significantly by SMAT. The maximum hardness is 270 HV 0.05  and the hardened layer thickness is about 0.6 mm after 40 min of SMAT. The increase in hardness of the samples is attributed to the surface martensite transformation, carbide precipitation, grain refinement and increased dislocation density.

sections.heading: Tensile properties
paragraphs:
The mechanical properties yield strength, tensile strength, % ductility and elastic modulus altered by surface mechanical attrition treatment were evaluated using tensile test as per ASTM  E8 , and  three  point bending tests as per ASTM  E855-08  respectively. The mechanical properties of HSLA steel altered by the severe plastic deformation of the surface are delineated in  Fig. 4 
                         .

As shown in  Fig. 4  the yield strength (Y.S.), ultimate tensile strength (U.T.S) and elastic modulus of steel is increasing with process time during the initial stage of processing and shows a decreasing trend thereafter. The yield strength increased from 258 MPa to 405 MPa in 20 min of SMAT and decreased to 388 MPa in 40 min treated samples. The changes in the mechanical properties are due to the complex effects hardening and softening mechanisms. The first stage of increment in Y.S., U.T.S. and elastic modulus is also contributed by carbide precipitation, increased dislocation densities and grain size. The coble creep dominating for nanocrystalline structures is responsible for decrement in Young's modulus beyond 30 min of treatment.

sections.heading: Wear behavior
paragraphs:
Fig. 5 
                          depicts the wear sliding wear behaviour of dual phase steel subjected to SMAT for different time period. As seen the sliding wear and wear rate of SMAT samples increased initially and decresed after a sliding distance of 1500 m. In fact very little wear occurred during the initial time period. Mechanical attrition creates a rough surface that increases wear rate initially. The wear resistance of the steel found increasing with the time of SMAT treatment. Wear resistant steel samples are found to increase with the time of SMAT exposure. Maximum wear resistant steel samples are found after 40 min of SMAT. This could be attributed to the martensite phases formed during SMAT.

sections.heading: Conclusions
paragraphs:
We demonstrated that SMAT could be used to design steel with a modified surface microstructure that results in mixed phases such as martensite and ferrite via stress induced transformation rather than an isothermal heat treatment. The following conclusions are obtained out the present study. 
                         
                            1. 
                            The SMAT treatment causes severe plastic deformation of the steel surface, which then results in a phase transformation. The percent transformation could be effectively controlled through process parameters. The DP steel subjected to 40 min of SMAT resulted in a microstructure consisting of 37% martensite and 63% ferrite. 
                         
                         
                            2. 
                            The transformation of equiaxed ferrite into bainitic ferrite resulted in shifting of x-ray peaks and the nano-crystallization has caused broadening. 
                         
                         
                            3. 
                            The hardness of the treated samples found varying across the cross section. A maximum surface hardness of 270 HV 0.05  is obtained at the surface while the core showed a hardness of 145 HV 0.05. 
                            
                         
                         
                            4. 
                            The SMAT had significantly altered the yield strength, tensile strength and Young's modulus of the steel, however the ductility is reduced.
